full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a little bit about what we’re doing to begin with. We’re interviewing second year women engineering students about their expectations of the placement, or, if they’re not going on placement why they’re not doing a placement and why they wanted to do engineering, and about their course so far really. And what we’re trying to do is improve the retention of women in the industry. So if it’s alright with you I’ll start by asking you some questions about your background and why you wanted to do the course that you’re doing and that. OK? Is it architectural engineering that you’re doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	And what ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did er physics, maths and design technology and then I did an ‘AS’ in chemistry and an ‘AS’ in geography.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Erm, I actually moved sc I – in my ‘A’ level years I actually moved schools and I went to [town] school, which is a private school. And its am all boys school up until sixth form, when it took girls.

Interviewer:	Was it just the sixth form that you went to that school then or were you in a private school before?

Subject:	I was in a private school before but that was an all girls school and we moved so I moved school.

Interviewer:	Yes, Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Not in the industry, no. Er, I did some engineering background because I did the engineering education scheme – I had chosen to do that, and we worked with [name] and worked on an engineering project but that was during my ‘A’ levels. It was an on-going project.

Interviewer:	OK, What do your parents do are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	My dad’s an engineer. He did production engineering. Erm, he originally did an apprenticeship but then he got asked – you know a couple of people were changing to a degree, you know and he went on to do production engineering.

Interviewer:	OK so when and how did you decide to do engineering?

Subject:	Erm, it was actually – I’ve always been into – interested in the engineering side of things but the architectural side of things interested me more but I knew that I’m not particularly arty and I knew that erm that I wouldn’t be good at all as a pure architect or something like that. And it’s actually – erm I’ve sort of found a course and it’s kind of pretty unique and it just looked something I really wanted to do. I think my dad probably influenced me a bit at school (yeah) and that type of thing is one of the few places with engineering basis but I’m not so technical to go into something like mechanical (yes) so I decided to sort of go for it.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have much careers advice or anything like that at school?

Subject:	Erm, not really. We did – you know the (Moreby?) tests and things like that where they tell you what you’re supposed to be good at, and things like that but no-one – I was very much sort of I want to do something that I’ll enjoy that kind of thing and not really thinking about the job.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think you would have gone into engineering if your dad wasn’t an engineer?

Subject:	Probably. Because I just – I always enjoyed maths, physics and design technology and it was always seemed to point towards that so, I think probably I still would have gone into it.

Interviewer:	Did you decide the direction you wanted to go in after you’d taken you’re ‘A’ levels or…?

Subject:	It was after but my ‘A’ levels I chose because I enjoyed it and it’s from those subjects that I ended up (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, and what sort of role do you think that the course that you went on played? Did you apply to go on the engineering education thing?

Subject:	No. It’s the type of thing – we displayed interest in it and essentially we were picked. So there were quite a few people that went for it and we were picked, and I mean, I applied for it – I didn’t – I thought it would be something good to do. I took it up because I was the (?) in a private school, at sixth form I needed to get a scholarship to go and so I actually got the design and technology scholarship and I think that helped. I was actually the first girl to get the design and technology scholarship at that school as well and I think that probably helped my case towards getting onto the engineering scheme.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of thing was involved in doing it?

Subject:	Well what we had to do – we went to [name] and we sort of went into a situation where actually – they make the boxes that contain circuit boards for the (?) and they actually were really doing it and what they were doing was workmen being workmen, you actually had to have 2 people handling it. That’s because they get so heavy and what they do is they’re just shifting it around by themselves and damaging them. And what we did was we created a turntable table that could actually hold the box, so it could rotate it, spin it round and it’s not a case of 2 people having to move it at some point. So erm that’s what we worked on. We ended up getting the gold crest award for that as well.

Interviewer:	OK, once you decided that you wanted to do this did you have much encouragement or did your dad put you off at all or was he happy that you wanted…?

Subject:	Oh yeah, I think he was very happy because I’ve, of course I was looking at all the universities and my dad being an engineering background, as soon as I mentioned [this university] was like definitely go to [this university], so I think he was very happy in the end, that I ended up coming here. Yeah, I got lots of encouragement.

Interviewer:	Ok, did you always know you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I did, ‘cos when I was in my first year I – erm you can’t help but think – it’s like you get to go on the fact that oh my God, it’s going to be really hard to get a placement and I always wanted to do it because er although I really enjoy my course, I’ve never had that much sort of focus, I mean my course is kind of orientated towards getting on site and having a role on site but also having the architectural basis behind it, so it’s going in 2 directions. And I was never quite sure – I always wanted my placement year to actually use it as – almost like an experiment to actually find out what I want to when I graduate.

Interviewer:	OK, did you realise that the subject was so male dominated?

Subject:	Er, I think I did. I knew that I was going to a male dominated area but er I was coming from a sixth form which was the majority of boys anyway. I mean I’ve always got on with lads, it doesn’t really phase me but I knew I was going to have a bit of a challenge on my hands.

Interviewer:	Yeah, was it strange going into that sort of male environment from being in a girls’ school?

Subject:	Hmm, I think it was a little bit, but I didn’t really – I didn’t really think of it that way. I’ve always got on with lads anyway – it wasn’t really a problem. No, I suppose it was, in the first like month or so there was – it was kind of strange – but luckily I went to the sixth form, with a couple of my best friends, so we were kind of cliquey as a girl group and then we got on with all the lads as well. Like I had – one lad that went to my school, lived down my road and so it was like…

Interviewer:	OK, did it ever bother you that there weren’t any women then, or weren’t many women?

Subject:	A little bit, like when I was – like when I did my physics. Both physics and design technology – I was the only girl in the group and so it is a challenge but then the teachers are always aware that you’re the only girl and like it’s really – it’s great because I was always the one conducting the experiments and stuff like that, so – it has its benefits at the same time, it’s always like oh, you’re just a girl you don’t know this kind of thing – so you have to prove yourself.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do engineering?

Subject:	I think so, I really do because er my course started out with 3 girls on it and now I’m the only girl left – 2 of the girls left.

Interviewer:	Out of how many?

Subject:	Er, yeah there were 3 of us, including myself.

Interviewer:	How many are on your course altogether?

Subject:	Oh, erm I think there’s about 18 or 20 I’m not sure – 16 or 18 maybe, something like that. But yeah, so it is fairly obvious that – my course, doing modules – it’s kind of obvious but and the worst thing is if I miss a lecture ‘cos I’m ill or something like that. Straight away they notice me – notice me missing, whereas if a couple of lads weren’t there, they wouldn’t notice them at all. So that is the down side of it.

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done to encourage more women?

Subject:	I think they – I – like when I was in the all girls school you just – it wasn’t – it wasn’t talked about. You er, we did our subjects and we did our career talks and things like that, to chose our ‘A’ levels and I didn’t do so many talks because I was moving. But at the same time, I can guarantee you most of my friends had never even – probably even talked about going into engineering. It was like – I don’t know, I’d just gone through the design side of it, if you know what I mean and they were going to be focussing on design – do you know what I mean? I think yeah – definitely – once I went to Solihull school, like people said why don’t you do engineering? And er, I think when it’s an all female environment it just doesn’t come into your heads, it’s when you’re around lads and realise that you actually maybe would be good at a sort of more blokey subject, if you know what I mean.

Interviewer:	Do you think then that there needs to be more information about what engineering is?

Subject:	Yeah because I mean even when into my interviews and did the Moreby test and things like that, there were loads of things like accounting for me, and I was just like – you can do something like that. Engineering never even just came up for me.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, determined – sort of very – you don’t have to – it’s a very er, when you (?) in it’s a very broad area, so the – you’ve got – especially the girls have got to have confidence. But I think determination, because there’s so many areas, and so many people that you’re dealing with - things like that and so many aspects to engineering, you can go wrong if you’re dealing with a particular project, and I think if you’ve got to just – be so positive really, like being sort of …

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those things that make a good engineer – do you think that men or women are better at any of those?

Subject:	I think we – there is probably the same as (?) – we do think very differently. And I’ll be the first one to admit that when I sit in there, with a group of lads they seem to have a lot more – er, it’s the way the lad’s brought up though – they go out with their dads and they tinker with cars and things like that. And I just didn’t do it – I wasn’t interested in it. And so I think probably lads are likely to have a lot more technical knowledge and so I’m finding I’m having to work quite hard to keep up really. And then I think girls have a better approach in the fact that they’re – they’re probably – they probably do the paperwork – and sometimes girls will like do the research you need to do, within a project, whereas lads just dive in. But I think they – well, I think as a team I think we work really well together. We’ve got all different – different types of methods that work together.

Interviewer:	Yeah, that’s great. You’ve said a bit about this already but what do you think are the main advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I think er one – it can be an advantage and a disadvantage is the fact that they’re very aware – if you’ve got a girl within the group, they’re very aware that they’ve got to include you – so it’s very good to get your point across, but at the same time, I think it’s still – because it is such a male dominated area, there’s such a lot of testosterone flying around and sometimes if you make a point – and maybe it’s not the best point in the world – they’ll be very quick to slap you down, you know. So I think – I mean even ‘cos I’ve got my placement sorted, I went for an interview and he was a really nice guy and he sat there chatting and one of the points he actually put across – he was very clear to make it very politically correct, but he said he liked to get girls into the office and I was like sort of, why is that then? And he said, I really like a male/female balance and although I’ll be working in the office it’s an architectural office, so I’ll be working in the architecture (section?), and I met the 2 girls that already work there, both of them are learning – they’re in interior design – they’re not actually in the engineering side of things – and it didn’t half me think that it was like, perhaps the girl thing kind of worked for me this time and it’s like – so you know.

Interviewer:	OK. We’ll talk a bit about the course then, has it been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. I – I tell you what I really enjoy with my course – I really – I mean of course there are some aspects that I just don’t get on with, its like there’s a couple of the modules that I find hard, but because it’s something I know I want to do, I’m prepared to work for it, sort of thing. And I do enjoy myself.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Er, I hate exams – that the really worst thing and er that was, like we’ve got six exams this semester. Erm, I’ve had a couple of modules, by a particular lecturer that have been really disorganised and I think that’s the worst bit – is when you sort of – even, if you don’t do the work fair enough, but when you actually put in the work and you’re sort of let down by a lecturer or something like that, that can annoy me a bit, but overall it’s been such a positive experience, I’ve really enjoyed it.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, I have – I’ve got – one of them – she’s not lecturing us but she’s – she’s a tutor on hand, if you know what I mean, we’ve got one particular module which – where – we’re actually designing a building for and she’s one of our consultants. We can go and see her. And then, last year, we had – oh actually we’ve got another one, this year, as well. She did half a module and she did – we’ve just finished with her. And then we’ve got – I had one last year as well.

Interviewer:	OK, Have you noticed any differences in the subjects that the women teach or the styles they teach – or like how they treat you? the female and male lecturers?

Subject:	Not particularly. Well – the thing – apart from the one that we’ve got the design group with, the other 2 lecturers I haven’t had a lot of contact with them – they’ve just been lecturing and maybe in tutorials we’ve been doing work and things like that. But those modules I’ve got on with OK. Erm, I think it can work for them, because I think there’s one I’ve had a bit of – a few problems with a bit of course work where we had to email the lecturer and he said don’t contact me personally ‘cos I’m acting as a client – and I went up to him and he said, ah, and I said I’m Natalie, you’ve been having a few problems with me and he’s like, oh it’s so great to put a face to the name – he was really nice to me but I couldn’t help thinking that maybe if it was a lad who’d done it, he would’ve been like, no, I told you not to contact me. So I think it can work for you.

Interviewer:	OK. Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Well it’s something I’d like to go in to, personally, because I looked into teaching as well. So I’m not going to go and be a (??) – I looked at the kind of teacher type of thing. Yeah, definitely, I think so.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that there aren’t more female lecturers then?

Subject:	I don’t know how the system works – I suppose you maybe have to go into teaching first before you could go into lecturing and I suppose engineering can be quite specialised. I obviously don’t really know, I couldn’t tell you.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the lecturers treat you the same as the lads on the course?

Subject:	I think the majority of the time they do because they I think they have to be aware of the balance between us and in my first year I actually – one of my lecturers emailed my personal tutor ‘cos I didn’t turn up for a lecture and I’d actually already emailed my personal tutor about it and I actually spoke to my lecturer about it and I said look – this isn’t fair, you’ve got something like 90 people in this lecture, you can’t possibly keep track of them, and there’s 2 girls and as soon as you notice I’m missing, you email my personal tutor when there’s was like, probably about 20 people missing that day, and it’s myself that gets victimised. And I think – I’d just make the point that perhaps, if he’s gonna do something like that, he’s going to have to take a register and be aware fair enough there’s one girl missing but there’s also like 20 lads missing. I think they have to be aware – ‘cos I actually spoke to him about that, and he said that’s fair enough, but at the same time – that’s your luck, if you know what I mean.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male

Interviewer:	Are you bothered about that at all, would you prefer a female?

Subject:	Not at all. He’s brilliant, I get on with him really well because I speak to him about the fact that I’ll be going away and he helped me out with the fact that I might miss a few deadlines, I had to schedule it round my deadlines and he was no, no, - he was really good.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Hmm, I don’t know. I think it’s probably – I live with 2 girls who are both engineers. I’ve got one – she’s a civil engineer, you’ve actually spoken to her before, and then I’ve got another girl who does aeronautical, and I think they influence me a lot because, lost words) and er, so, well – maybe it’s just chemistry and things like that. But still, I think we’re all like a support system for each other. Although you’re on different courses, we’re all – we all like sort of work, you know, in a male dominated environment and I think we – you know – definitely support each other in that respect. My personal tutor’s also really good.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had to do much group work?

Subject:	Loads, loads. It’s kind of – this semester, it’s kind of doing my head in a little bit, because we’ve only got one module where we’re not doing group work and – although – yeah, I do think it is a good thing, to have team work but at the same time I think it – sometimes it can reflect badly on those who have put loads of work in and you always get the ones who just go along for the ride. And I know they do peer assessment but it’s very hard, although they say, do your marks, put them in – it just doesn’t matter. It’s very hard, when you’re sitting there, in a group and you’re having your peer assess each other and say, well actually everyone got 10 apart from you – you got 5. It’s not (hard?) especially when they’re people on your course. And you’re gonna have – you know you’re gonna have another year and a half with them, or whatever. So…

Interviewer:	Do you think that it would be better if you had more women to work with or (lost words)?

Subject:	No, I honestly don’t think it makes a difference, ‘cos although erm I think – I don’t think it depends on whether you’re male or female – the amount of work that you do – erm, no I don’t think it – I think some – females generally work better – work harder but erm I think in the particular groups I’m in – I’ve always got a few that work really hard and then a few that won’t buck up, and I don’t think it actually works better if I had girls in the group.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particular good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Er, I had – it was two last year – the first year, what they do – the worst thing is - they put in you register order and put you in groups, so you’re always in the same group. And it’s just like you sit there and go and there’s lecturers coming in and out going (?) – don’t worry, we’ll organise you. You don’t have to get yourself into groups, and we look at each other and we’re like oh I’m gonna be with you again am I? And last year, there was – the first semester we worked with on a particular project and we were put in groups of 4. And myself and er my best friend on my course, we were in a group together and with these two other lads – and they did do some work but most of the time it was us two doing the tasks and (lost words). We were working through the project ourselves and we’d had – it wasn’t the case that they wouldn’t do any work but we had to allocate them the work to do. But then at the same time I was with them again in the second – second semester, we were actually with – civil engineering was the module and er we got put into groups again and we ended up with a couple of er civil engineers who had like a couple years out and were much older, and they just took charge of the module, they told us what to do and we were probably working at the pace that we worked for the other group, but because they were so experienced they told us what to do, when to do it, and we got brilliant marks for the project but at the same time we sat there and were, like, we can’t really input as much as them because they’ve had so much more experience than us, so there’s sort of 2 sides to sort of quirkiness.

Interviewer:	Did they treat you both the same, or do you think…?

Subject:	It is the same – because bearing in mind we had 2 who were all civils and then us two that were architectural and I think that’s the only split they saw. The only split they saw was the fact that we’ve got ours – 2 from architectural engineering, 2 from civil engineering and that’s the only split they saw.

Interviewer:	OK, are there any parts of the teaching and advice that you’ve had that you think will help you on your placement particularly?

Subject:	No erm I don’t think we’ve had as much help as we could have – finding the placement. Erm, I mean the guys in civil engineering were generally brilliant at organising the talks and things like that but when it came down to interview techniques and things like that, we got no help at all, and I think the one thing we probably could have done with a bit of help on was that – when I’m actually – in an individual situation and I’m in a job situation, and it’s not quite like this –it’s gonna be – I think I could probably do with more help on my interview skills.

Interviewer:	OK. What about in terms of the actual skills that you’ll take from the course, to the placement?

Subject:	I can’t actually say until I get into the placement because I haven’t actually been given a job title (no). I know I’ll be working in an office and one of the main skills I’ll have to use is er work on CAD and computer – computer skills really because I know I’ll be given designs, and I’ll have to produce them and things like that, so I think that’s the main skill I’ll end up using and we had a whole module on that, in the first year.

Interviewer:	What about skills that probably aren’t technical, like team work and things like that?

Subject:	I don’t think we’ve really – I mean I’ve worked on them, because I’ve been on courses and things like that but I don’t think – I think it will help – the group work will definitely help in that because you I have – you always have to communicate with different types of people and I think that is definitely one of the benefits of group work, say.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that any of your previous work experience will help you on your placement, or…?

Subject:	Erm, not really – when it comes to things like team work, then it’s fair enough but I don’t think I can actually say that I’m taking –lots of work skills, you know, because I still can’t say what exactly I’m going to be doing.

Interviewer:	OK, fine do you feel like your ready to go on placement now?

Subject:	I’m really looking forward to it (yeah) in fact I’m really looking forward – particularly because, I don’t think I could’ve done 3 years straight studying because even now I’m thinking I really want to get out there and actually use what I’ve learnt, in a work situation, because you don’t really get to do that. Erm I’m really looking forward to that one.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any part of the educational experience and the way that you’re taught, is going to reflect what it’s really like in the industry? Or do you think it will be different?

Subject:	I don’t know. We’ve got so many teachers that who were – who are like really realistic and they – you can tell they’ve been out there and they’ve been on site, because they – in some ways you think they – I don’t think you can actually say until you’ve – you’ve been in the situation, do you know what I mean? Erm, unfortunately, I think I’ll have the opportunity to get out on site and we are taught a lot about the – the erm conditions on site and how that site actually works and, to be honest, I’ll be working in an office most of the time – I’ll be like in the background. But I think where I will have the opportunity and I’d really like to actually experience it because there’s quite a few lads on my course who actually got out there – they know people and they’ve been able to work there for the summer and I know – part of me is like (passing the site?) and I’ve never really experienced it so.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that work will differ from being at university in like terms of how you’re treated and things like that?

Subject:	Erm, I think it’s probably going to be completely different environment, because I think I’ll be treated as if – I mean here, you’ve got deadlines, you’ve got things you’ve got to do in your spare time. I think this will be a case of you will be working in a team, permanently, so it’s not – I mean fair enough, you’ve got individuals on site to try and reach certain goals but I don’t think erm, I think you’ll always have someone around if you know what I mean, to fall back on whereas in here you get an individual project, you do it, you hand it in, it’s marked, that’s it. You don’t necessarily get a lot of feedback and I think that being in a work environment will be slightly different but at the same time we’ll be able to use other skills such as team work I guess.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide that you wanted to go on placement?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know – is it bad that it’s money orientated? I er – no, I think it was nice because I think I might feel a little bit restless if I did the 3 year degree and I think it’s nice that I’ll actually be able to get – get out and actually experience it and I’ll be able to come back in my 3rd year and go well, I’ve got all this input now, I can reflect it in my work, in my dissertation – whatever. So er, yeah, I think I – I don’t know I think it’s good getting out there and actually using what I’ve learnt.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know where you’re going on placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m working for [company] which are part of [company] and they’re the (?) consultants for their architectural side of things. So I’ll be working on things like commercial building and things like that.

Interviewer:	OK what attracted you to them?

Subject:	Er, I applied to a number of firms – I applied to a few consultancies and I applied to a few actual construction companies and to be honest erm there were 2 consultancies – I was more interested in the consultancy work because I can’t really see myself walking – I mean I can see myself like doing work on site, but I can’t see myself running the site or anything like that. Erm, but er it’s actually [company] that contacted me first and I went into the interview – and it was a very casual interview and they offered me the job while I was just sitting there. And erm, to be honest, they were so efficient and it was so easy to sort everything out – the interview was (?) for me, it was fine. And it seemed to be that all the other companies I’ve contacted said oh, we’ll contact you in spring. It seems to be very – a very kind of laid back situation about it and er, I was like that’s the kind of environment I want to work in, where everything’s so organised, I know what I’m doing, I know I’ll be treated well whereas er I mean I’ve got three that are still sort of sending emails saying oh your application’s still being processed. And I’m like well how is this company – I actually applied through [company], which is the construction company and they put me onto [company]. And how are they so organised to get their placements sorted and the others are still, oh we’ll contact when ever sort of thing? So I think – and also it’s 20 minutes from my home so – that helps as well.

Interviewer:	When you were looking at the companies you applied to – not just [placement company], did you look at like the type of work that you would be doing and things like the training opportunities and …?

Subject:	I did – well er my big thing was opportunities after I graduate. Because I think there’s loads – certainly, it’s quite a scary the statistic - I don’t know what it is – however many graduates can’t get work now, so I mean I think luckily being in engineering and they’re so desperate for engineering students, but at the same time I think that was one of the benefits. But I actually er I did a – I looked generally into the consultancies but er it was also management roles, such as project management roles and things like that, that I went into. I actually went into the (?) that did the engineering recruitment like (lost words) and things like that, and I actually managed to speak to quite a few people personally so I had a chance to find out what sort of – because industrial placements is kind of a – it’s very varied what you might be doing. You might be working all hours on a site and then you might be just picking up and making tea. So I did look at the criteria for what I’ll be doing and things like that. Although I haven’t got a specific erm – a specific role at the moment, I will be – I know roughly what I will be doing.

Interviewer:	Did you have the opportunity at all to be sponsored on – for your course?

Subject:	Erm, I didn’t look into it, to be honest. Erm, I – I actually didn’t apply to go to UCAS till quite late and I didn’t apply until my January results came through and they were actually better – much better than I thought they would be. So if I wanted to speak to (?) – I didn’t actually, so it was kind of a come round, look at all the universities as fast as I could, choose my courses – you know what I mean? And so, once I got into the first 6 months of the uni, I hadn’t really thought of it all until my friend Amy actually got sponsored. But to be honest I think er with my course it’s quite – it’s not – I mean it’s not brand new but it’s quite new and it’s kind of interesting to employers and they’re not quite sure, whereas something like civil engineering, which has been going on years and years and then they know they’ve got a good thing with civil engineering. So I think the opportunity – I wanted to wait for - the opportunity will arise when I’ve proved myself during my placement year, and maybe get sponsored in my final year (OK) something like that. I did ask in the interview, what the opportunities were and he said, well if you like the place and we get on with you, I don’t see why we can’t sponsor you in the final year. We’ll have to see.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about the placement? Or what are you mainly looking forward to and what are you worried about?

Subject:	I’m mainly looking forward to actually getting into the design process, being able to sit there and have my input on a building that might be built – that’s really kind of exciting. The worst thing will be making tea. It would be dogsbody – it would be, I hate to say it but a glorified secretary – I’d hate that. 

Interviewer:	Is that a worry because you’re a student and only there for a year, or because you’re a woman or both?

Subject:	I think it’s a bit of both. I think mainly it might be because I’m a student and them going oh, we’ve got another placement student – oh a dogsbody situation, but I think being a girl might also reflect on that a little bit.

Interviewer:	In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	I have no idea. And while that scares me a little bit at the same time it kind of excites me because I’m like – I think, that the whole process of this placement – the fact that I’m going to be able to actually decide what I want to do. And it will actually sort of –I’ll actually be able to determine whether I like what I’m doing or whether it’s a situation where I might want to be able to (?) by the end of my placement – so, I can’t actually tell you.

Interviewer:	Do you think you’d like to go into management side of things or become more specialised?

Subject:	Probably. I can probably see myself going into management – yeah, definitely. Like we do management modules and I’ve always enjoyed doing in those and then I think when I’m working in a team environment, although I try not to, I do tend to er – erm I’m quite bossy as a character – it’s a good thing that I know it, so I kind of stop myself now and then but I think most of the time I like to be in control of the situation.

Interviewer:	OK, what would you say would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	Oh God. Erm, probably something like a Head of Architectural Design in a big firm such as [company]. Not, maybe not Head of Architecture – top Architectural Consultant, or anything Architectural Engineering Consultant in a company like – the top (?)

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s a realistic goal or…?

Subject:	I think so – definitely. I know it takes – it’s gonna take years and years but I think I could do it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties on your way?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, probably but er you can’t possibly say – I don’t think you could possibly say you’ll just breeze through. You’re always gonna encounter difficulties. You’re always gonna encounter people you don’t get on with, or people that take liberties. And, as a girl, I think you have to be stronger because - especially with men – there are men out there that still think that – I don’t know – that they’re better than women. And I think it’s very important that women are – have to be educated on the fact that they’re going to be treated differently, although it’s hard and you shouldn’t be – I think er, you have to be aware that you’re different. I think.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	I do because erm one of the main things that – when I was in the interview, was the fact that, the hardest thing when I was applying, I had to write a letter about my course and you say you’re doing civil engineering – they know exactly what you’re doing; they know exactly what they’re getting. So I had lots of people emailing me, saying oh thanks for the application but can you tell me about your course? And I think that’s the main thing really, I was sitting in the interview and the guy said they’ve never taken on an architectural engineering student before, they’ve always gone for architecture. And he said, I really am interested to see how your course will differ and how you’ve been taught will differ – so I think I’ve er kind of got to set a precedence, because I think if I reflect well he might come back and look for more architectural engineering students. But I mean, I’m glad I’m not going into pure architecture – I can’t remember who I was speaking to, because architecture is a very male dominated area, it’s very rare that you get female architects so… I think there’s 2 aspects now – I’ve got architecture and engineering, and they’re both male dominated environments. So, I suppose I want to prove myself.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	No, I don’t think so. I think I’ve done – I’ve done OK. I’ve got to see with this placement, but I’m so looking forward to it. It’ll take a lot to knock my er knock my confidence, in that effect.

Interviewer:	Yeah, it sounds really exciting. We’re coming to the end now, what 5 words would you use to describe like the culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry?

Subject:	Oh, that’s very hard. I don’t think you could limit it to 5 words because I don’t think it’s a black and white industry. I don’t think you can say oh it’s – I don’t know. I don’t know –it’s a positive industry – because, you can’t – I think pre – different people have different experiences. I don’t think er – you can limit it to 5 words – I can’t think. I don’t know – it is – it is male dominated. You can’t help but accept that. The only thing is – I don’t know – I think being female does work for you. Hmm, well – it’s a hard question.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that it is so masculine? Do you think that’s just because of the numbers of men, or is it more than that?

Subject:	Maybe it’s just – I don’t know. I think it’s maybe the way boys are brought up. I think boys and girls – it’s like I’d be the first one to admit that, like, as I said earlier, I was not – as a child I would not have been interested in sitting in the garage, with my dad, looking at the car, whereas boys are automatic – it’s just the way – I think it’s the way we’re brought up. And going to really an all girls school, once again engineering was not – well, it wasn’t really talked about as in – we did the sciences, we did the maths, we did the arts. And I don’t think – I don’t think you can ever stop that divide. I think you can learn to accept it, you know what I mean.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will get better then, or do you think it will…?

Subject:	I think it will because I think, at the moment, you’ve still got generations within the engineering environment, that are sexist, and there’s nothing you can do about it. But – and also that’s the way they were brought up, like years ago. It’s like women shouldn’t work, kind of thing. And it’s – but I think, as the years go on, I see it – my generation – even like – my teachers at the boys school were very, very aware of it, and if anything they could go a bit too far and they gave – the girls kind of got to take liberties. They were very aware of it. Erm, so, I think maybe as I go through my career, and sort of as my generation goes through it, I think it will generally get better, because that’s the way we’re being taught now. It’s kind of hard to taught – teach the people who are high up in industry, who have been dong the same thing they’ve been doing, for years. Yes, I think it will get better.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll tell you a little bit about what we’re doing to begin with. We’re interviewing second year women engineering students about their expectations of the placement, or, if they’re not going on placement why they’re not doing a placement and why they wanted to do engineering, and about their course so far really. And what we’re trying to do is improve the retention of women in the industry. So if it’s alright with you I’ll start by asking you some questions about your background and why you wanted to do the course that you’re doing and that. OK? Is it architectural engineering that you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what ‘A’ levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did er physics, maths and design technology and then I did an ‘AS’ in chemistry and an ‘AS’ in geography.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I actually moved sc I – in my ‘A’ level years I actually moved schools and I went to [town] school, which is a private school. And its am all boys school up until sixth form, when it took girls.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it just the sixth form that you went to that school then or were you in a private school before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was in a private school before but that was an all girls school and we moved so I moved school.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not in the industry, no. Er, I did some engineering background because I did the engineering education scheme – I had chosen to do that, and we worked with [name] and worked on an engineering project but that was during my ‘A’ levels. It was an on-going project.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What do your parents do are either of them engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My dad’s an engineer. He did production engineering. Erm, he originally did an apprenticeship but then he got asked – you know a couple of people were changing to a degree, you know and he went on to do production engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK so when and how did you decide to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was actually – I’ve always been into – interested in the engineering side of things but the architectural side of things interested me more but I knew that I’m not particularly arty and I knew that erm that I wouldn’t be good at all as a pure architect or something like that. And it’s actually – erm I’ve sort of found a course and it’s kind of pretty unique and it just looked something I really wanted to do. I think my dad probably influenced me a bit at school (yeah) and that type of thing is one of the few places with engineering basis but I’m not so technical to go into something like mechanical (yes) so I decided to sort of go for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you have much careers advice or anything like that at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. We did – you know the (Moreby?) tests and things like that where they tell you what you’re supposed to be good at, and things like that but no-one – I was very much sort of I want to do something that I’ll enjoy that kind of thing and not really thinking about the job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think you would have gone into engineering if your dad wasn’t an engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably. Because I just – I always enjoyed maths, physics and design technology and it was always seemed to point towards that so, I think probably I still would have gone into it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you decide the direction you wanted to go in after you’d taken you’re ‘A’ levels or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was after but my ‘A’ levels I chose because I enjoyed it and it’s from those subjects that I ended up (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what sort of role do you think that the course that you went on played? Did you apply to go on the engineering education thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. It’s the type of thing – we displayed interest in it and essentially we were picked. So there were quite a few people that went for it and we were picked, and I mean, I applied for it – I didn’t – I thought it would be something good to do. I took it up because I was the (?) in a private school, at sixth form I needed to get a scholarship to go and so I actually got the design and technology scholarship and I think that helped. I was actually the first girl to get the design and technology scholarship at that school as well and I think that probably helped my case towards getting onto the engineering scheme.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of thing was involved in doing it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well what we had to do – we went to [name] and we sort of went into a situation where actually – they make the boxes that contain circuit boards for the (?) and they actually were really doing it and what they were doing was workmen being workmen, you actually had to have 2 people handling it. That’s because they get so heavy and what they do is they’re just shifting it around by themselves and damaging them. And what we did was we created a turntable table that could actually hold the box, so it could rotate it, spin it round and it’s not a case of 2 people having to move it at some point. So erm that’s what we worked on. We ended up getting the gold crest award for that as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, once you decided that you wanted to do this did you have much encouragement or did your dad put you off at all or was he happy that you wanted…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah, I think he was very happy because I’ve, of course I was looking at all the universities and my dad being an engineering background, as soon as I mentioned [this university] was like definitely go to [this university], so I think he was very happy in the end, that I ended up coming here. Yeah, I got lots of encouragement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, did you always know you wanted to do a sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I did, ‘cos when I was in my first year I – erm you can’t help but think – it’s like you get to go on the fact that oh my God, it’s going to be really hard to get a placement and I always wanted to do it because er although I really enjoy my course, I’ve never had that much sort of focus, I mean my course is kind of orientated towards getting on site and having a role on site but also having the architectural basis behind it, so it’s going in 2 directions. And I was never quite sure – I always wanted my placement year to actually use it as – almost like an experiment to actually find out what I want to when I graduate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you realise that the subject was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think I did. I knew that I was going to a male dominated area but er I was coming from a sixth form which was the majority of boys anyway. I mean I’ve always got on with lads, it doesn’t really phase me but I knew I was going to have a bit of a challenge on my hands.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, was it strange going into that sort of male environment from being in a girls’ school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I think it was a little bit, but I didn’t really – I didn’t really think of it that way. I’ve always got on with lads anyway – it wasn’t really a problem. No, I suppose it was, in the first like month or so there was – it was kind of strange – but luckily I went to the sixth form, with a couple of my best friends, so we were kind of cliquey as a girl group and then we got on with all the lads as well. Like I had – one lad that went to my school, lived down my road and so it was like…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did it ever bother you that there weren’t any women then, or weren’t many women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A little bit, like when I was – like when I did my physics. Both physics and design technology – I was the only girl in the group and so it is a challenge but then the teachers are always aware that you’re the only girl and like it’s really – it’s great because I was always the one conducting the experiments and stuff like that, so – it has its benefits at the same time, it’s always like oh, you’re just a girl you don’t know this kind of thing – so you have to prove yourself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, I really do because er my course started out with 3 girls on it and now I’m the only girl left – 2 of the girls left.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Out of how many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah there were 3 of us, including myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many are on your course altogether?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, erm I think there’s about 18 or 20 I’m not sure – 16 or 18 maybe, something like that. But yeah, so it is fairly obvious that – my course, doing modules – it’s kind of obvious but and the worst thing is if I miss a lecture ‘cos I’m ill or something like that. Straight away they notice me – notice me missing, whereas if a couple of lads weren’t there, they wouldn’t notice them at all. So that is the down side of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be done to encourage more women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they – I – like when I was in the all girls school you just – it wasn’t – it wasn’t talked about. You er, we did our subjects and we did our career talks and things like that, to chose our ‘A’ levels and I didn’t do so many talks because I was moving. But at the same time, I can guarantee you most of my friends had never even – probably even talked about going into engineering. It was like – I don’t know, I’d just gone through the design side of it, if you know what I mean and they were going to be focussing on design – do you know what I mean? I think yeah – definitely – once I went to Solihull school, like people said why don’t you do engineering? And er, I think when it’s an all female environment it just doesn’t come into your heads, it’s when you’re around lads and realise that you actually maybe would be good at a sort of more blokey subject, if you know what I mean.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think then that there needs to be more information about what engineering is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah because I mean even when into my interviews and did the Moreby test and things like that, there were loads of things like accounting for me, and I was just like – you can do something like that. Engineering never even just came up for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, determined – sort of very – you don’t have to – it’s a very er, when you (?) in it’s a very broad area, so the – you’ve got – especially the girls have got to have confidence. But I think determination, because there’s so many areas, and so many people that you’re dealing with - things like that and so many aspects to engineering, you can go wrong if you’re dealing with a particular project, and I think if you’ve got to just – be so positive really, like being sort of …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those things that make a good engineer – do you think that men or women are better at any of those?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think we – there is probably the same as (?) – we do think very differently. And I’ll be the first one to admit that when I sit in there, with a group of lads they seem to have a lot more – er, it’s the way the lad’s brought up though – they go out with their dads and they tinker with cars and things like that. And I just didn’t do it – I wasn’t interested in it. And so I think probably lads are likely to have a lot more technical knowledge and so I’m finding I’m having to work quite hard to keep up really. And then I think girls have a better approach in the fact that they’re – they’re probably – they probably do the paperwork – and sometimes girls will like do the research you need to do, within a project, whereas lads just dive in. But I think they – well, I think as a team I think we work really well together. We’ve got all different – different types of methods that work together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, that’s great. You’ve said a bit about this already but what do you think are the main advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think er one – it can be an advantage and a disadvantage is the fact that they’re very aware – if you’ve got a girl within the group, they’re very aware that they’ve got to include you – so it’s very good to get your point across, but at the same time, I think it’s still – because it is such a male dominated area, there’s such a lot of testosterone flying around and sometimes if you make a point – and maybe it’s not the best point in the world – they’ll be very quick to slap you down, you know. So I think – I mean even ‘cos I’ve got my placement sorted, I went for an interview and he was a really nice guy and he sat there chatting and one of the points he actually put across – he was very clear to make it very politically correct, but he said he liked to get girls into the office and I was like sort of, why is that then? And he said, I really like a male/female balance and although I’ll be working in the office it’s an architectural office, so I’ll be working in the architecture (section?), and I met the 2 girls that already work there, both of them are learning – they’re in interior design – they’re not actually in the engineering side of things – and it didn’t half me think that it was like, perhaps the girl thing kind of worked for me this time and it’s like – so you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. We’ll talk a bit about the course then, has it been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. I – I tell you what I really enjoy with my course – I really – I mean of course there are some aspects that I just don’t get on with, its like there’s a couple of the modules that I find hard, but because it’s something I know I want to do, I’m prepared to work for it, sort of thing. And I do enjoy myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I hate exams – that the really worst thing and er that was, like we’ve got six exams this semester. Erm, I’ve had a couple of modules, by a particular lecturer that have been really disorganised and I think that’s the worst bit – is when you sort of – even, if you don’t do the work fair enough, but when you actually put in the work and you’re sort of let down by a lecturer or something like that, that can annoy me a bit, but overall it’s been such a positive experience, I’ve really enjoyed it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I have – I’ve got – one of them – she’s not lecturing us but she’s – she’s a tutor on hand, if you know what I mean, we’ve got one particular module which – where – we’re actually designing a building for and she’s one of our consultants. We can go and see her. And then, last year, we had – oh actually we’ve got another one, this year, as well. She did half a module and she did – we’ve just finished with her. And then we’ve got – I had one last year as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Have you noticed any differences in the subjects that the women teach or the styles they teach – or like how they treat you? the female and male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not particularly. Well – the thing – apart from the one that we’ve got the design group with, the other 2 lecturers I haven’t had a lot of contact with them – they’ve just been lecturing and maybe in tutorials we’ve been doing work and things like that. But those modules I’ve got on with OK. Erm, I think it can work for them, because I think there’s one I’ve had a bit of – a few problems with a bit of course work where we had to email the lecturer and he said don’t contact me personally ‘cos I’m acting as a client – and I went up to him and he said, ah, and I said I’m Natalie, you’ve been having a few problems with me and he’s like, oh it’s so great to put a face to the name – he was really nice to me but I couldn’t help thinking that maybe if it was a lad who’d done it, he would’ve been like, no, I told you not to contact me. So I think it can work for you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it’s something I’d like to go in to, personally, because I looked into teaching as well. So I’m not going to go and be a (??) – I looked at the kind of teacher type of thing. Yeah, definitely, I think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that there aren’t more female lecturers then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know how the system works – I suppose you maybe have to go into teaching first before you could go into lecturing and I suppose engineering can be quite specialised. I obviously don’t really know, I couldn’t tell you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the lecturers treat you the same as the lads on the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the majority of the time they do because they I think they have to be aware of the balance between us and in my first year I actually – one of my lecturers emailed my personal tutor ‘cos I didn’t turn up for a lecture and I’d actually already emailed my personal tutor about it and I actually spoke to my lecturer about it and I said look – this isn’t fair, you’ve got something like 90 people in this lecture, you can’t possibly keep track of them, and there’s 2 girls and as soon as you notice I’m missing, you email my personal tutor when there’s was like, probably about 20 people missing that day, and it’s myself that gets victimised. And I think – I’d just make the point that perhaps, if he’s gonna do something like that, he’s going to have to take a register and be aware fair enough there’s one girl missing but there’s also like 20 lads missing. I think they have to be aware – ‘cos I actually spoke to him about that, and he said that’s fair enough, but at the same time – that’s your luck, if you know what I mean.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you bothered about that at all, would you prefer a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not at all. He’s brilliant, I get on with him really well because I speak to him about the fact that I’ll be going away and he helped me out with the fact that I might miss a few deadlines, I had to schedule it round my deadlines and he was no, no, - he was really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I don’t know. I think it’s probably – I live with 2 girls who are both engineers. I’ve got one – she’s a civil engineer, you’ve actually spoken to her before, and then I’ve got another girl who does aeronautical, and I think they influence me a lot because, lost words) and er, so, well – maybe it’s just chemistry and things like that. But still, I think we’re all like a support system for each other. Although you’re on different courses, we’re all – we all like sort of work, you know, in a male dominated environment and I think we – you know – definitely support each other in that respect. My personal tutor’s also really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had to do much group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Loads, loads. It’s kind of – this semester, it’s kind of doing my head in a little bit, because we’ve only got one module where we’re not doing group work and – although – yeah, I do think it is a good thing, to have team work but at the same time I think it – sometimes it can reflect badly on those who have put loads of work in and you always get the ones who just go along for the ride. And I know they do peer assessment but it’s very hard, although they say, do your marks, put them in – it just doesn’t matter. It’s very hard, when you’re sitting there, in a group and you’re having your peer assess each other and say, well actually everyone got 10 apart from you – you got 5. It’s not (hard?) especially when they’re people on your course. And you’re gonna have – you know you’re gonna have another year and a half with them, or whatever. So…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it would be better if you had more women to work with or (lost words)?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I honestly don’t think it makes a difference, ‘cos although erm I think – I don’t think it depends on whether you’re male or female – the amount of work that you do – erm, no I don’t think it – I think some – females generally work better – work harder but erm I think in the particular groups I’m in – I’ve always got a few that work really hard and then a few that won’t buck up, and I don’t think it actually works better if I had girls in the group.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particular good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I had – it was two last year – the first year, what they do – the worst thing is - they put in you register order and put you in groups, so you’re always in the same group. And it’s just like you sit there and go and there’s lecturers coming in and out going (?) – don’t worry, we’ll organise you. You don’t have to get yourself into groups, and we look at each other and we’re like oh I’m gonna be with you again am I? And last year, there was – the first semester we worked with on a particular project and we were put in groups of 4. And myself and er my best friend on my course, we were in a group together and with these two other lads – and they did do some work but most of the time it was us two doing the tasks and (lost words). We were working through the project ourselves and we’d had – it wasn’t the case that they wouldn’t do any work but we had to allocate them the work to do. But then at the same time I was with them again in the second – second semester, we were actually with – civil engineering was the module and er we got put into groups again and we ended up with a couple of er civil engineers who had like a couple years out and were much older, and they just took charge of the module, they told us what to do and we were probably working at the pace that we worked for the other group, but because they were so experienced they told us what to do, when to do it, and we got brilliant marks for the project but at the same time we sat there and were, like, we can’t really input as much as them because they’ve had so much more experience than us, so there’s sort of 2 sides to sort of quirkiness.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they treat you both the same, or do you think…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is the same – because bearing in mind we had 2 who were all civils and then us two that were architectural and I think that’s the only split they saw. The only split they saw was the fact that we’ve got ours – 2 from architectural engineering, 2 from civil engineering and that’s the only split they saw.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are there any parts of the teaching and advice that you’ve had that you think will help you on your placement particularly?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No erm I don’t think we’ve had as much help as we could have – finding the placement. Erm, I mean the guys in civil engineering were generally brilliant at organising the talks and things like that but when it came down to interview techniques and things like that, we got no help at all, and I think the one thing we probably could have done with a bit of help on was that – when I’m actually – in an individual situation and I’m in a job situation, and it’s not quite like this –it’s gonna be – I think I could probably do with more help on my interview skills.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What about in terms of the actual skills that you’ll take from the course, to the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can’t actually say until I get into the placement because I haven’t actually been given a job title (no). I know I’ll be working in an office and one of the main skills I’ll have to use is er work on CAD and computer – computer skills really because I know I’ll be given designs, and I’ll have to produce them and things like that, so I think that’s the main skill I’ll end up using and we had a whole module on that, in the first year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about skills that probably aren’t technical, like team work and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think we’ve really – I mean I’ve worked on them, because I’ve been on courses and things like that but I don’t think – I think it will help – the group work will definitely help in that because you I have – you always have to communicate with different types of people and I think that is definitely one of the benefits of group work, say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that any of your previous work experience will help you on your placement, or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really – when it comes to things like team work, then it’s fair enough but I don’t think I can actually say that I’m taking –lots of work skills, you know, because I still can’t say what exactly I’m going to be doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, fine do you feel like your ready to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m really looking forward to it (yeah) in fact I’m really looking forward – particularly because, I don’t think I could’ve done 3 years straight studying because even now I’m thinking I really want to get out there and actually use what I’ve learnt, in a work situation, because you don’t really get to do that. Erm I’m really looking forward to that one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any part of the educational experience and the way that you’re taught, is going to reflect what it’s really like in the industry? Or do you think it will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. We’ve got so many teachers that who were – who are like really realistic and they – you can tell they’ve been out there and they’ve been on site, because they – in some ways you think they – I don’t think you can actually say until you’ve – you’ve been in the situation, do you know what I mean? Erm, unfortunately, I think I’ll have the opportunity to get out on site and we are taught a lot about the – the erm conditions on site and how that site actually works and, to be honest, I’ll be working in an office most of the time – I’ll be like in the background. But I think where I will have the opportunity and I’d really like to actually experience it because there’s quite a few lads on my course who actually got out there – they know people and they’ve been able to work there for the summer and I know – part of me is like (passing the site?) and I’ve never really experienced it so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that work will differ from being at university in like terms of how you’re treated and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it’s probably going to be completely different environment, because I think I’ll be treated as if – I mean here, you’ve got deadlines, you’ve got things you’ve got to do in your spare time. I think this will be a case of you will be working in a team, permanently, so it’s not – I mean fair enough, you’ve got individuals on site to try and reach certain goals but I don’t think erm, I think you’ll always have someone around if you know what I mean, to fall back on whereas in here you get an individual project, you do it, you hand it in, it’s marked, that’s it. You don’t necessarily get a lot of feedback and I think that being in a work environment will be slightly different but at the same time we’ll be able to use other skills such as team work I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you decide that you wanted to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know – is it bad that it’s money orientated? I er – no, I think it was nice because I think I might feel a little bit restless if I did the 3 year degree and I think it’s nice that I’ll actually be able to get – get out and actually experience it and I’ll be able to come back in my 3rd year and go well, I’ve got all this input now, I can reflect it in my work, in my dissertation – whatever. So er, yeah, I think I – I don’t know I think it’s good getting out there and actually using what I’ve learnt.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know where you’re going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m working for [company] which are part of [company] and they’re the (?) consultants for their architectural side of things. So I’ll be working on things like commercial building and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK what attracted you to them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I applied to a number of firms – I applied to a few consultancies and I applied to a few actual construction companies and to be honest erm there were 2 consultancies – I was more interested in the consultancy work because I can’t really see myself walking – I mean I can see myself like doing work on site, but I can’t see myself running the site or anything like that. Erm, but er it’s actually [company] that contacted me first and I went into the interview – and it was a very casual interview and they offered me the job while I was just sitting there. And erm, to be honest, they were so efficient and it was so easy to sort everything out – the interview was (?) for me, it was fine. And it seemed to be that all the other companies I’ve contacted said oh, we’ll contact you in spring. It seems to be very – a very kind of laid back situation about it and er, I was like that’s the kind of environment I want to work in, where everything’s so organised, I know what I’m doing, I know I’ll be treated well whereas er I mean I’ve got three that are still sort of sending emails saying oh your application’s still being processed. And I’m like well how is this company – I actually applied through [company], which is the construction company and they put me onto [company]. And how are they so organised to get their placements sorted and the others are still, oh we’ll contact when ever sort of thing? So I think – and also it’s 20 minutes from my home so – that helps as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you were looking at the companies you applied to – not just [placement company], did you look at like the type of work that you would be doing and things like the training opportunities and …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did – well er my big thing was opportunities after I graduate. Because I think there’s loads – certainly, it’s quite a scary the statistic - I don’t know what it is – however many graduates can’t get work now, so I mean I think luckily being in engineering and they’re so desperate for engineering students, but at the same time I think that was one of the benefits. But I actually er I did a – I looked generally into the consultancies but er it was also management roles, such as project management roles and things like that, that I went into. I actually went into the (?) that did the engineering recruitment like (lost words) and things like that, and I actually managed to speak to quite a few people personally so I had a chance to find out what sort of – because industrial placements is kind of a – it’s very varied what you might be doing. You might be working all hours on a site and then you might be just picking up and making tea. So I did look at the criteria for what I’ll be doing and things like that. Although I haven’t got a specific erm – a specific role at the moment, I will be – I know roughly what I will be doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have the opportunity at all to be sponsored on – for your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn’t look into it, to be honest. Erm, I – I actually didn’t apply to go to UCAS till quite late and I didn’t apply until my January results came through and they were actually better – much better than I thought they would be. So if I wanted to speak to (?) – I didn’t actually, so it was kind of a come round, look at all the universities as fast as I could, choose my courses – you know what I mean? And so, once I got into the first 6 months of the uni, I hadn’t really thought of it all until my friend Amy actually got sponsored. But to be honest I think er with my course it’s quite – it’s not – I mean it’s not brand new but it’s quite new and it’s kind of interesting to employers and they’re not quite sure, whereas something like civil engineering, which has been going on years and years and then they know they’ve got a good thing with civil engineering. So I think the opportunity – I wanted to wait for - the opportunity will arise when I’ve proved myself during my placement year, and maybe get sponsored in my final year (OK) something like that. I did ask in the interview, what the opportunities were and he said, well if you like the place and we get on with you, I don’t see why we can’t sponsor you in the final year. We’ll have to see.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about the placement? Or what are you mainly looking forward to and what are you worried about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m mainly looking forward to actually getting into the design process, being able to sit there and have my input on a building that might be built – that’s really kind of exciting. The worst thing will be making tea. It would be dogsbody – it would be, I hate to say it but a glorified secretary – I’d hate that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that a worry because you’re a student and only there for a year, or because you’re a woman or both?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s a bit of both. I think mainly it might be because I’m a student and them going oh, we’ve got another placement student – oh a dogsbody situation, but I think being a girl might also reflect on that a little bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have no idea. And while that scares me a little bit at the same time it kind of excites me because I’m like – I think, that the whole process of this placement – the fact that I’m going to be able to actually decide what I want to do. And it will actually sort of –I’ll actually be able to determine whether I like what I’m doing or whether it’s a situation where I might want to be able to (?) by the end of my placement – so, I can’t actually tell you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’d like to go into management side of things or become more specialised?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably. I can probably see myself going into management – yeah, definitely. Like we do management modules and I’ve always enjoyed doing in those and then I think when I’m working in a team environment, although I try not to, I do tend to er – erm I’m quite bossy as a character – it’s a good thing that I know it, so I kind of stop myself now and then but I think most of the time I like to be in control of the situation.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would you say would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh God. Erm, probably something like a Head of Architectural Design in a big firm such as [company]. Not, maybe not Head of Architecture – top Architectural Consultant, or anything Architectural Engineering Consultant in a company like – the top (?)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s a realistic goal or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so – definitely. I know it takes – it’s gonna take years and years but I think I could do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties on your way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, probably but er you can’t possibly say – I don’t think you could possibly say you’ll just breeze through. You’re always gonna encounter difficulties. You’re always gonna encounter people you don’t get on with, or people that take liberties. And, as a girl, I think you have to be stronger because - especially with men – there are men out there that still think that – I don’t know – that they’re better than women. And I think it’s very important that women are – have to be educated on the fact that they’re going to be treated differently, although it’s hard and you shouldn’t be – I think er, you have to be aware that you’re different. I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do because erm one of the main things that – when I was in the interview, was the fact that, the hardest thing when I was applying, I had to write a letter about my course and you say you’re doing civil engineering – they know exactly what you’re doing; they know exactly what they’re getting. So I had lots of people emailing me, saying oh thanks for the application but can you tell me about your course? And I think that’s the main thing really, I was sitting in the interview and the guy said they’ve never taken on an architectural engineering student before, they’ve always gone for architecture. And he said, I really am interested to see how your course will differ and how you’ve been taught will differ – so I think I’ve er kind of got to set a precedence, because I think if I reflect well he might come back and look for more architectural engineering students. But I mean, I’m glad I’m not going into pure architecture – I can’t remember who I was speaking to, because architecture is a very male dominated area, it’s very rare that you get female architects so… I think there’s 2 aspects now – I’ve got architecture and engineering, and they’re both male dominated environments. So, I suppose I want to prove myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think so. I think I’ve done – I’ve done OK. I’ve got to see with this placement, but I’m so looking forward to it. It’ll take a lot to knock my er knock my confidence, in that effect.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, it sounds really exciting. We’re coming to the end now, what 5 words would you use to describe like the culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, that’s very hard. I don’t think you could limit it to 5 words because I don’t think it’s a black and white industry. I don’t think you can say oh it’s – I don’t know. I don’t know –it’s a positive industry – because, you can’t – I think pre – different people have different experiences. I don’t think er – you can limit it to 5 words – I can’t think. I don’t know – it is – it is male dominated. You can’t help but accept that. The only thing is – I don’t know – I think being female does work for you. Hmm, well – it’s a hard question.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that it is so masculine? Do you think that’s just because of the numbers of men, or is it more than that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe it’s just – I don’t know. I think it’s maybe the way boys are brought up. I think boys and girls – it’s like I’d be the first one to admit that, like, as I said earlier, I was not – as a child I would not have been interested in sitting in the garage, with my dad, looking at the car, whereas boys are automatic – it’s just the way – I think it’s the way we’re brought up. And going to really an all girls school, once again engineering was not – well, it wasn’t really talked about as in – we did the sciences, we did the maths, we did the arts. And I don’t think – I don’t think you can ever stop that divide. I think you can learn to accept it, you know what I mean.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will get better then, or do you think it will…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will because I think, at the moment, you’ve still got generations within the engineering environment, that are sexist, and there’s nothing you can do about it. But – and also that’s the way they were brought up, like years ago. It’s like women shouldn’t work, kind of thing. And it’s – but I think, as the years go on, I see it – my generation – even like – my teachers at the boys school were very, very aware of it, and if anything they could go a bit too far and they gave – the girls kind of got to take liberties. They were very aware of it. Erm, so, I think maybe as I go through my career, and sort of as my generation goes through it, I think it will generally get better, because that’s the way we’re being taught now. It’s kind of hard to taught – teach the people who are high up in industry, who have been dong the same thing they’ve been doing, for years. Yes, I think it will get better.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything. Thank you.
